summary:
Belarusian law treats transgender visibility as criminal material. In April 2024 the definition of pornography was amended to bring depictions of same-sex relationships and of transgender people inside it, and a Ministry of Culture decree issued the same year grouped "homosexualism" with paedophilia and necrophilia under the category of "non-traditional relationships". Production and distribution carry up to four years' imprisonment, rising to thirteen years where children are involved. Prosecution proceeds under Article 343 of the Criminal Code. Human Rights Watch described the change as an explicit attack on the dignity of LGBT people. The offence attaches to depiction rather than conduct, so a trans person's own image or public presence can be treated as pornographic material.

An April 2026 law bans propaganda of homosexual relations, gender reassignment, childlessness and paedophilia. The inclusion of gender reassignment means that advocacy of, or representation of, transition falls within the prohibition. The Prosecutor General's Office has announced plans for a further administrative-penalty law against "LGBTI propaganda"; it had not been tabled at the time of the ILGA-Europe review for 2024.

Enforcement has been immediate. TG House Belarus reported that more than fifteen LGBTQ+ people were detained in September 2024 alone, eight of them transgender; most were charged with hooliganism and two with pornography. Those held reported physical and psychological abuse in custody, and some left the country afterwards. Activists say police beat LGBTQ+ people while arresting and charging them and that charges are coerced.

Foreign visitors are exposed through the same machinery. In 2004, when an international gay and lesbian festival was targeted, the authorities made threatening telephone calls stating that foreigners attending workshops and discussions would be immediately expelled under the article on intervention in domestic affairs. A trans visitor attending meetings or events connected to LGBT organising can expect the same treatment.

Belarus offers no protection against persecution on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Persecution on the basis of sexual orientation is not recognised in Belarusian law as a ground for refugee status, and partners are not recognised for immigration purposes, so a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no immigration route here. No anti-discrimination protection exists and there is no prohibition of hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Belarus is not a member of the Council of Europe, so there is no appeal to the European Court of Human Rights.

Official hate-crime data is not published. Belarus has not reported hate-crime data to the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights since 2015 and has no National Point of Contact for that reporting; figures for 2024 come from civil-society organisations including Human Constanta. Police do not register brutality cases against sexual minorities or investigate homophobic motives, and officers collect personal data, passport details and photographs of gay people at known cruising areas, as reported by Vstrecha in Brest and Gomel.

Transgender people who suffer violence have little expectation of redress. In September 2008 two transgender men raped in Minsk did not report to police because they were unsure police would help. Detention carries a further risk: in prisons, homosexuality is subject to speculation, blackmail and extortion, gay and lesbian prisoners are largely unprotected, and turnkeys often encourage other prisoners to abuse them.

LGBT venues have been closed, raided or tolerated only intermittently. The gay club Oskar was closed by the authorities in February 2000 and its owner Ivan Suchinski was later killed; riot police raided a 1999 pride party; police have carried out unprovoked actions in bars frequented by homosexuals in Gomel and Minsk.

Psychological care is scarce. Qualified psychological help is generally unavailable and no trans-specific facilities are documented.

Public opinion is hostile. A Pew Research Center survey in May 2017 found that 84 per cent of Belarusians believed homosexuality should not be accepted by society and 81 per cent opposed same-sex marriage, with 16 per cent in favour. A 2002 Lambda Belarus survey found that 47 per cent thought gay people should be imprisoned, and many Belarusians treat homosexuality as a psychiatric illness. Among younger people attitudes are comparatively less hostile but still largely negative: the 2017 poll found 22 per cent of younger respondents in favour of legal gay marriage against 14 per cent of older ones, and a 2007 vote of young people in Gomel region found that 47.6 per cent held negative feelings towards sexual and gender minorities and 10 per cent wanted homosexual relations criminalised. Gay life is largely underground, most LGBT people conceal their orientation in public, and those who are open face harassment and physical violence.

State propaganda reinforces the climate. State television has equated LGBTI identities with paedophilia and described them as "a weapon in the hands of the West", and TG House recorded an increase in hate speech in state propaganda. A new National Security Concept emphasises "traditional values". ILGA-Europe recorded that at least ten transgender people left Belarus in a year because of discrimination and repression.
tangentialFactors:
Critics of the April 2026 propaganda law compare it to Russia's 2013 law against propaganda of non-traditional sexual relations. The 2024 decree's grouping of homosexualism with paedophilia and necrophilia follows the same rhetorical pattern of equating LGBT identity with harm to children.

Within the OSCE region's hate-crime reporting rounds, Belarus files no data and has no designated point of contact, leaving civil-society organisations as the only source for incidents recorded against LGBT people.
localsOnly:
Belarusian law does not recognise persecution on the basis of sexual orientation as a ground for refugee status, so LGBT residents have no domestic protection route and must seek asylum abroad. After the end of communist rule many Belarusians sought and received political asylum, most often citing formal or informal police harassment; Amnesty International and AILGBT-Belarus documented individuals granted asylum in the Czech Republic, France, the Netherlands and Sweden.

The constitutional guarantee of equality before the law, Article 22, has not protected LGBT people in practice; the wider environment includes a clampdown on civil society, harassment of activists, arbitrary detention, and retention of the death penalty. The three Minsk universities offering full psychology courses, Belarus State University, Belarus Pedagogical University and the European Humanities University, do not address the problems of sexual minorities.

No official organisation represents gay and lesbian people in Belarus, and other initiatives work outside the legal framework. Pride events between 1999 and 2010 were repeatedly banned, raided or forcibly prevented.
outOfScopeNotes:
Figures on detentions and abuse in custody rest on reporting by non-governmental organisations and activists and have no official confirmation; the state publishes no hate-crime data.

Whether the April 2026 law is in force and how its provisions are applied to foreign visitors is not established in the available sources.

The sources do not describe the procedure for legal gender recognition in Belarus, or whether foreign identity documents recording a gender different from that assigned at birth are accepted at the border, in hotels or in dealings with officials.

No transgender-specific accommodation or care facilities are documented, and no findings on youth-specific access to care are recorded.
